messages.author: 42eed4e1caba0ad0
messages.subject: Session management in RApache
parts:
Hi lads,

I'm about to create a simple webapp... well, more like tool, for
importing non-native data formats in R. Practically, it's a wrapper
for foreign package. I need some recommendations regarding session
management. Since RApache supports only stateless script execution, I
need to apply some hack in order to keep the session "alive". The
import tool I previously mentioned is only a part of a large-scale
project, so please focus on session management, rather than the app
"per se".

Any suggestions should suffice!

Thanks,
Alex

messages.author: 98e634f62928ae87
messages.subject: Re: Session management in RApache
parts:
Hi,

after having read a short conversation about this "problem" on the list, I tried to make up some kind of solution.

  1) First, I tried to make R/Apache work with only a single child (as MPV worker), but as Jeff pointed out this would let to a single threated webserver, which could be a great performance disaster. If the webapp would not be under heavy load stressed by multiple users at the same time, this trade-off could work.

  2) Next, I tried to make this environment somehow capable of multi-user sessions, and I figured out a quite ugly and not favorable hack which could work thought. Caution: do not read this paragraph if you have a weak heart :) Anyway, I thought about setting up several Rapache instances with low dedicated resources (this could be several separate webserver on the same host, a virtualized environment with small guests or small instances in a cloud), and a central one, which does the session management. This central server with a database backend held the user's settings and datasets also, and dynamically partition the job between the separate Rapache servers. Of course a user's request would always get to the same worker, so loading data is done only once, it is a "live session" as you wrote. I know it is a bit hackish way and may not be a piece of cake to install an environment like that, but would work for sure - as I think. Opinions?

  3) To save the complexity of the second design, I went forth, and has the question in mind: does a "live session" really worth this? Live session is useful to load data only once and also for not storing the same data in several places (in several R sessions) in the same time, so for saving resources. This could be done in another, more simple way - but may not work for every application design of course. Loading a decent or even a midsized dataset can take significant amount of time, and an application cannot afford the laziness to load a dataset for 1-2 seconds after every request (of course just in the first 30-60 request depending on the Apache settings). But that would be a shame :) A hack could be, if a user opens a data, then a script would load it in all sessions (Apache children) also. Well, it is a big resource waste, and after children dieing and new ones starting the data has to be loaded again.
That could be saved I think with changing the idea of loading data. In a webapp, the most common case is to load a dataset to draw a plot, compute univariate statistics, or to fit some models with a low number of variables. These techniques does not require the whole dataset, but others might need it (that is why this alternative is not an option for some webapp designs). I made some basic experiment and research in the subject (based on some similar impulses), which could be found on SO, and I found that there are two way to run. First, importing datasets in any format, convert them to binary files and later always loading those, OR second, import the dataset to a database (MySQL in the example), and always fetch only the required columns of the data. My small experiment (what I plan to investigate further with a reliable and accurate methodology in the near future) showed, that loading binary data was a hundred way (!!) faster than importing SPSS sav files, and fetching only a few variables from MySQL could also be an option, thought just after reading in the dataset first time.
After a few days, I strange idea came to my mind, that combining the two method could speed up the loading process and made up a tiny "package" which saves the data frames or lists to a special, binary file (all variables are saved in a single Rdata file which is archived to a tar file in the end), and via the loads function, it is possible to load only the required variables of a dataset. This process had another huge performance advance (loading only 2 columns of a 600 columned data frame was about 100 times faster with the not-so-well optimized "package"), so contrast to loading SPSS sav files (was more than 2 secs) loading only a few columns can be done in a few millisecond.
This time interval should not count in a webapp :)
And also: always loading only the required variables of a dataset means a lower load on the server. Of course, this could depend on the goal of the webapp.

I am still not pleased with the latter potential "solution" (well, solution might be for me) and working on the issue. I made up a small package (saves), as mentioned before, and have several features in my mind, which could speed up/optimize the process. And of course: any suggestion is welcome!

Also: any warning would make me happy which would point out that my idea is totally wrong.

Best,
Gergely

messages.author: 98e634f62928ae87
messages.subject: Re: Session management in RApache
parts:
I think Jeroen propose the idea of calling Rserve from Rapache, as Rserve does not have a fully functional Php client yet (which could manage sessions), but Rapache can call the (Rserve) R client to start/detach/attach/close an R session and also to eval commands in that.
The downside of this - if I understand correctly - that the setup is a bit complicated: in your Rhtml files you have to attach to or start an Rserve session and RSeval every command (or a series of them), at the end detaching from it (if you willing to keep the session) and saving the session information outside of Rapache. After a sensible idle time the session could be shut down if no formal logout was made.

In essence: this sounds great, thank you Jeroen! Forget the proposals I wrote an hour ago to the list, this way seems a lot more rational. Though, I still feel the importance of speeding up the loading time of datasets :)

Best regards,
Gergely

Nah it just saves and loads workspaces. This happens in less then 0.1s for a dataset of say 10mb so its not worth going through the trouble of real statefulness. You should only do that if you want to do very much computations on one session, and your workspace is too big to write/read to disk.
